title: Leslie Vs. April

jokes.text: Leslie says Ben will be the 'first gentleman' if she wins the presidency in 2024, and Ben says 'Actually, that sounds kind of great.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is projecting decades into the future about being president, mapping out East and West Wings
jokes.punchline: Ben's sincere enthusiasm for being a supportive spouse rather than any ambition of his own — warmly self-deprecating
jokes.explanation: Works because it's deeply character-specific — Ben's gentle, supportive personality makes his genuine delight at being 'first gentleman' feel earned. Leslie's casual presidential ambition is also a perfect character note. The joke is in the sincerity, not irony.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We could be in the White House by 2020.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Even 2024 is ambitious.

jokes.text: Leslie meets the Vice President and says 'You're — my name just came out of your mouth.'
jokes.setup: Leslie, a political superfan, is introduced to an actual Vice President who knows her name
jokes.punchline: Her starstruck verbal disintegration — she can't process the reality of her hero knowing who she is
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character integration. Leslie is the consummate government professional who completely loses her composure meeting a political idol. The line captures her short-circuiting brain in the most economical, perfectly worded way. It's specific to Leslie and specific to the moment.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: When we're in the White House, you'll be the First Gentleman.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I think you mean First Lady.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, First Gentleman. You're a gentleman, and you'll be first.

jokes.text: Leslie immediately volunteers to take over as Secretary of State when the VP begins to pay her a compliment.
jokes.setup: The VP is about to give Leslie a standard congratulatory speech
jokes.punchline: Leslie jumps to 'I couldn't possibly take Madam Secretary Clinton's position' — assuming a job offer that was never made
jokes.explanation: Perfect Leslie Knope joke. She is so ambitious and so flustered that she immediately assumes any compliment from a VP is a Cabinet offer. The escalation from starstruck to 'I'll do it' is a textbook character comedy beat that only works for this specific character.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I got you an engagement present.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Is it a solid gold statue of me? Or a lifetime supply of waffles? Or a solid gold waffle of me?

jokes.text: Leslie tells the VP 'You're very handsome' in the middle of a formal diplomatic exchange.
jokes.setup: The VP and Leslie are exchanging polite thank-yous in an official context
jokes.punchline: Leslie, still flustered, blurts out that he's handsome — her filter completely gone
jokes.explanation: The cap on the VP sequence. Leslie's filter is completely gone and what comes out is pure mortifying admiration. The handlers rushing to end the meeting makes it cringe-funny. Works as escalation of existing joke rather than a wholly original beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Did you guys hear that? He said my name. Vice President Biden said my name!

jokes.text: Leslie tells the Secret Service agent: 'You don't let anything happen to him, you understand me? He is precious cargo.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is leaving after meeting the VP, speaking to his security detail
jokes.punchline: She gives them orders about protecting the VP as if she's the one in charge — classic Leslie overreach delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: The perfect button on the VP sequence. Leslie's complete unself-awareness — giving orders to Secret Service agents about protecting the VP as if that's her job — is quintessential Leslie Knope. 'Precious cargo' is a wonderfully absurd phrase delivered with complete sincerity. High quotability, high character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, well, that's very flattering, but I'm not sure I'm really qualified for... wait, did you say Deputy Director? I'm in.

jokes.text: Ben describes his new job's perks: 'Three weeks of vacation, matching 401(K), and a pretty sweet windbreaker.'
jokes.setup: Ben is listing the benefits of his impressive new accounting job to build to why it's a great package
jokes.punchline: The list culminates in a 'pretty sweet windbreaker' — the windbreaker doesn't belong in the same sentence as real benefits, and Ben says it with the same weight as the others
jokes.explanation: Classic rule-of-three subversion. The windbreaker is funny because it's simultaneously too small a perk and because Ben treats it as equivalent to the real benefits. Good economy, solid structure, and works with Ben's accountant sensibility.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're welcome, Mr. Vice President. It was an honor to serve alongside you.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And I just want to say, your leadership has been truly inspiring. The way you've handled environmental policy, it's really—it's really something special.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And your tie today, it's a very nice shade of blue. Really brings out your—it brings out the blue in your eyes, which are very blue.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Anyway, I'm just going to stop talking now. So... thank you.

jokes.text: Ben's talking head: 'So just call me Bond, municipal bond.'
jokes.setup: Ben explains he's going back to accounting for a stable life before marriage
jokes.punchline: The James Bond wordplay pivot — 'municipal bond' as a pun on Bond/bond, delivered with total self-satisfaction
jokes.explanation: It's a groan-worthy pun, but the joke is really about Ben's nerd pride — he's clearly delighted with himself, which makes it endearing. The follow-up in the next scene (it 'killed at the accounting firm') perfectly completes the joke by confirming only other accountants would laugh at this.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm treating Ben like he needs protection from the Vice President.

jokes.text: 'Yeah, that joke killed at the accounting firm.'
jokes.setup: Ben delivered the 'municipal bond' pun to presumably no reaction from Tom/Chris
jokes.punchline: Ben confirms in the next beat that this joke did go over great — but exclusively with accountants, which only deepens how dorky the whole thing is
jokes.explanation: This line is the actual punchline to the pun — the callback confirms Ben's obliviousness to how dorky he is. The scene cut makes it land harder. Perfect economy: six words do all the work. It retroactively makes the pun funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm back in accounting. It's like James Bond, except instead of fighting supervillains, I'm fighting... spreadsheets. And instead of a martini, I have a cup of coffee. And instead of a tuxedo, I have this shirt from Banana Republic.

jokes.text: Tom greets Tom and Chris: 'Well, well, well. If it isn't Mr. Looks and Professor Books. He's Looks. I got it.'
jokes.setup: Tom wants to pitch his business idea to Ben and Chris
jokes.punchline: Tom assigns Chris 'Mr. Looks' and Ben 'Professor Books,' then immediately explains himself — the self-annotation undermines the cool entrance he was going for
jokes.explanation: Tom's tendency to make unnecessarily elaborate entrances is well-established. The self-satisfied 'He's Looks. I got it' is the right touch of Tom over-explaining his own bit. Works because it's character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I made a joke about municipal bonds. The accountants laughed so hard, one of them had to sit down. I'm not saying it was the funniest thing ever said, but it was definitely top five, easily.

jokes.text: Chris delivers escalating 'facts': 'Fun fact: Ben just got an amazing accounting job. Regular fact: I have to go to a meeting. Un-fun fact: My Uncle just had a stroke.'
jokes.setup: Chris has categorized information into 'fun facts' and follows the formula
jokes.punchline: The third category, 'un-fun fact,' ends with something genuinely terrible — delivered with the same chipper Chris Traeger energy
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is immaculate: fun fact (positive), regular fact (neutral), un-fun fact (devastating). The escalation catches the audience off guard, and the deadpan delivery of a stroke as merely an 'un-fun fact' is perfectly calibrated dark comedy. Highly quotable, structurally excellent, deeply character-specific to Chris's relentless positivity meeting something genuinely sad.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ben, you're 'The Debt Tornado.' Andy, you're 'The Silly Goose.'

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yes! I'm the Silly Goose!

jokes.text: Tom's business pitch: he's going to rent 'upscale clothing to middle school kids, because I discovered I'm roughly the same size as the average Pawnee 12-year-old.'
jokes.setup: Tom is pitching a legitimate business concept about renting clothes to kids who outgrow them
jokes.punchline: The reveal that his insight came from discovering he's the same size as a 12-year-old — a both self-deprecating and absurd admission
jokes.explanation: The business idea is actually clever, but the real joke is Tom's casual self-revelation that he's the size of a 12-year-old Pawnee kid. It's absurd and self-deprecating simultaneously, which is a hard balance. Character-specific because Tom's vanity makes this admission even funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Fun facts: the Great Wall of China is visible from space, honey badgers are immune to snake venom, and your father had a second family in Manitoba.

jokes.text: April's presentation uses stats: 'Washington D.C. has more dog parks per capita than most cities.' Ben responds: 'Can you say per capita again? I want to take a picture of you saying per capita.'
jokes.setup: April is giving a serious, competent presentation about dog parks
jokes.punchline: Ben is so delighted and proud that April said 'per capita' correctly that he wants to photograph it — sweet and condescending in equal measure
jokes.explanation: Warm character comedy — Ben's dorky enthusiasm for April's professional development is charming. The specific word 'per capita' is funny because it's such an unremarkable data term to be excited about. Works on the relationship dynamics level.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm leveraging my core competencies to create a synergistic paradigm shift in the value-added solutions space.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head: 'April came to me with an idea to build a dog park in Pawnee. I recognized her potential a long time ago, and she's finally living up to it. I mean, I am so proud of her, I could cry. And... here we go.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is proudly claiming credit for April's development in a confessional
jokes.punchline: 'And... here we go' — Leslie announcing her own imminent crying as if observing it happen to someone else, utterly self-aware
jokes.explanation: Beautifully constructed. Leslie is so earnest that she starts crying, but then the joke is the clinical self-narration: 'And... here we go.' It treats her own emotional outburst as a known phenomenon she's observing from a distance. Perfect economy, highly quotable, deeply Leslie-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I rent out my clothes to other guys. It's a business model that works because I'm a very small man.

jokes.text: Leslie critiques April's appearance — April reveals the goth look is 'publicity for Orin's new performance art show. He's an animal living on a human farm. And you can go and feed him from your own hand.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been trying to take April under her wing and critique her professional image
jokes.punchline: It's not April's personal style — it's body paint for a performance art show where a man lives as an animal and people hand-feed him
jokes.explanation: Orin as a recurring absurdist figure is well-used here. The specificity of 'animal living on a human farm' and being able to hand-feed him is maximally creepy and funny. April's complete nonchalance about it makes it work.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: One of the 'dog parks' is actually just a parking lot.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Ugh, that's horrifying, and so is Orin. You should not be friends with him.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just heard about Orin's performance art
jokes.punchline: Leslie's reaction includes both a critique of the art AND a direct personal attack on Orin as a person, said flatly
jokes.explanation: Quick, functional. The flat delivery of 'you should not be friends with him' as an adult authority figure seriously advising this is the joke. Competent but not special.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Per capita.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, say that again.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Per capita.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh man, that's so hot. Can you say it one more time while I take a picture?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Please? Per capita is my new thing.

jokes.text: Leslie invokes 'dibs' as a legal concept: 'I've been doing slow, painstaking work so I don't want to whip out the legalese on you now, but I got dibs.'
jokes.setup: April has just proposed Lot 48 for the dog park — the lot Leslie has been trying to develop for years
jokes.punchline: Leslie's legal threat is 'dibs' — she frames playground logic as serious legal precedent
jokes.explanation: Leslie is someone who lives by the rules and proper procedure — so her retreating to 'dibs' while calling it 'legalese' is a great character-specific irony. Well-constructed, good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to cry. I'm going to cry right now.

jokes.text: Andy sits down at his desk, stares at his computer, says 'Okay, something is different about my computer.' Long pause. 'Aha. It's gone.'
jokes.setup: Andy's computer has been stolen from his desk
jokes.punchline: Andy takes a beat — a notably long pause — to identify what's different, then arrives at the obvious conclusion with triumphant 'Aha'
jokes.explanation: The [05:04] and [05:09] timestamp gap suggests a real comedic pause between 'something is different' and 'It's gone.' Andy's detective instincts treating the absence of a computer as a solvable riddle is perfect for his character — he's essentially Sherlock Holmes without the intelligence. The 'Aha' as a triumphant conclusion is the cherry on top.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Orin has been working on a performance art piece where he stands in the town square wearing a bikini made of raw chicken, and he just screams about his childhood for six hours straight.

jokes.text: Andy announces: 'A game is the foot.'
jokes.setup: Andy has realized his computer is stolen and is about to begin investigating
jokes.punchline: He mangles 'the game is afoot' into 'a game is the foot' — confident delivery of a scrambled idiom
jokes.explanation: Andy-as-detective-movie-character is perfect. The malapropism of 'a game is the foot' is the right level of wrong — close enough to reveal he knows the reference but doesn't quite understand it. Economical and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm prepared to take this all the way to court. I have documented everything in triplicate, filed the appropriate forms, and I'm ready to pursue this with the full force of municipal code section 47-B, paragraph 3, subsection...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: ...which clearly states: 'Dibs.' I called dibs on this lot first, and according to the ancient laws of childhood, that makes it mine. Finders keepers, losers weepers.

jokes.text: Andy discovers his sunglasses were also stolen: 'They got my sunglasses too. I was in Miami last weekend. I took my talents to South Beach.'
jokes.setup: Andy is tallying up what was taken from his desk
jokes.punchline: The sunglasses prompt a LeBron James reference — Andy quotes LeBron's infamous 'I'm taking my talents to South Beach' press conference about his own Miami trip
jokes.explanation: Andy applying a LeBron-level grandiose phrase to going on a regular vacation is a classic absurdist juxtaposition. Works on Andy's character — he genuinely means it. The cultural reference has dated somewhat but was sharp at the time.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: The game is a foot.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, no. The game is... afoot? No, that's not right either. The game is... a-foot? Like, the game has a foot?

jokes.text: Andy sarcastically accuses Tom: 'How do you spend your time in Miami? Maybe fencing stolen computers?' Tom: 'Yes, I took your government computer from Indiana to Miami to sell it on the black market for 150 bucks.'
jokes.setup: Andy is 'investigating' and suspects Tom
jokes.punchline: Tom sarcastically confesses in the most detailed, incriminating way possible — $150 is an absurdly low amount to fence a computer, making the whole premise ridiculous
jokes.explanation: Tom's sarcastic over-confession is funny, and '$150' is the right absurdly specific low number. Andy then taking it literally makes it better.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I went to Miami for vacation. Best decision I ever made. I'm not going back to Pawnee. I'm taking my talents to South Beach.

jokes.text: Andy tells Tom: 'Ha-ha, you don't know it, but you just gave yourself away.' — treating a sarcastic fake confession as an actual slip.
jokes.setup: Tom sarcastically 'confessed' in obvious joke form
jokes.punchline: Andy interprets it literally as an accidental self-incrimination, full detective pride
jokes.explanation: The punchline to the sarcastic confession. Andy's oblivious triumph — certain he's outfoxed Tom through Tom's own slip — is the perfect Andy move. Works because it reveals Andy's detective playacting is completely earnest.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Yeah, I stole your computer. I'm running a very profitable business stealing government computers and selling them for seven dollars each on Craigslist.

jokes.text: Tom reviewing April's mission statement: 'Gotta say, I'm impressed. Your mission statement made sense, and you didn't use one R. Kelly lyric.'
jokes.setup: Tom is reviewing April's business proposal for the dog park
jokes.punchline: Tom's highest praise includes 'you didn't use one R. Kelly lyric' — implying his previous standard included expecting R. Kelly lyrics in mission statements
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Tom considers R. Kelly lyric inclusion something to watch out for — implying he's encountered it before. Specific, absurd, and funny as a low bar for a compliment. The R. Kelly reference has aged poorly given later revelations, but as written it's a solid bit.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Tom, this business plan is actually really impressive. You've thought through all the details, the financials, the marketing strategy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Thanks, Ben. I'm really proud of it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Just one thing though—please tell me there are no R. Kelly lyrics in here.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Why would there be R. Kelly lyrics in a business plan?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Because the last time you got excited about something, you wouldn't stop quoting 'I believe I can fly' at the city council meeting.

jokes.text: Tom proposes the industrial site: 'You know, I think any of the four previous locations would work, but there's something about this place. It just has a really good energy here, you know? Lots of natural light.' Ben/others: 'It's tiny and awful and loud. And it's zone 14B, industrial waste clean-up site.'
jokes.setup: Tom is enthusiastically pitching an industrial waste site as a dog park location
jokes.punchline: Everything specific about it is terrible — the others list concrete horrible facts while Tom talks about vibes
jokes.explanation: Standard optimist-vs-reality joke. Tom's 'good energy' and 'natural light' framing against an industrial waste site is a reliable structure but not especially original.

jokes.text: 'We should technically be wearing Hazmat suits right now. It seems like the kind of place a ska band would go to shoot heroin.'
jokes.setup: The group is standing in zone 14B, an industrial waste site
jokes.punchline: Ben's escalation from 'Hazmat suits' to the very specific image of 'a ska band shooting heroin' — an oddly precise cultural reference about the worst possible recreational setting
jokes.explanation: The ska band/heroin image is unexpectedly specific and funny — ska is an inherently goofy genre associated with the late 90s, so the image of ska musicians shooting heroin in an industrial waste site is maximally absurd. 'Technically' before 'Hazmat suits' is great deadpan. High quotability. One of the episode's sharpest lines.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What is that thing?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh my God. That's my childhood doll.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Why would you leave that here?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I didn't! I threw it away years ago.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Come on, guys, this is a great place for a dog park. I mean, look, there's already a dog here.' The 'dog' is a terrifying doll.
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to sell the industrial site; a 'dog' appears to support his case
jokes.punchline: It's not a dog — it's a horrifying doll, which Ben recognizes from childhood as traumatic
jokes.explanation: Strong visual gag — the 'dog' being a terrifying doll doubles down on how wrong this location is. Ben's trauma response ('This is traumatic for me') adds a nice personal layer. Works better on screen than on paper.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Leslie, I need you to get me a helicopter.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A helicopter? April, that's not really—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: And I need you to teach it to speak French.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, now you're just—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Also, I want you to go back in time and prevent the invention of Mondays.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's literally impossible.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: And finally, I need you to make Jerry the mayor of a small European country.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, why would you—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Actually, that's the only reasonable one.

jokes.text: April bargaining: 'Saw off your pinky toe. / No. / Shave your head. / No. / Have sex with Jerry. / No. / Well, I tried to be reasonable.'
jokes.setup: Leslie says she'll 'do anything' to keep April from bringing Lot 48 to city council
jokes.punchline: April's 'anything' list escalates from unpleasant (lose a toe) to humiliating (shave head) to 'have sex with Jerry' — then April frames these as reasonable requests
jokes.explanation: April's dark sadism toward Jerry is well-established and the escalation is perfectly calibrated. The kicker — 'Well, I tried to be reasonable' — reframes the entire list as April actually trying to compromise. Classic April character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've created a monster. April has become too efficient, too capable. She's like Frankenstein's monster, except instead of terrorizing villagers, she's just... perfectly organizing my files and anticipating my needs before I even know I have them.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's the job description.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know, but I didn't think you'd actually be GOOD at it. Now I'm afraid if I say the wrong thing, you'll turn on me. I've lost control of my creation.

jokes.text: Leslie to Joe (her therapist dog or someone calming): 'What do I do, Joe?' Joe stares at her. Leslie: 'God, he's good.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is asking for advice from 'Joe' about dealing with April
jokes.punchline: Joe appears to be a dog (or someone who gives advice non-verbally), and Leslie is genuinely calmed and impressed by the non-response
jokes.explanation: The implication that Leslie consults a dog (named Joe) for professional advice, and finds it effective, is charmingly absurd. 'God, he's good' treats the non-response as expert guidance.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So Ricky is... well, he's very masculine. Deep voice, facial hair, very strong.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Sounds like a man.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: He is! Except when he needs to be a woman for the mission.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That doesn't make any sense.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know, but we're committed to the bit.

jokes.text: Ron: 'I didn't. You just walked in here and started talking.'
jokes.setup: Leslie says 'Ron, thank you for agreeing to see me'
jokes.punchline: Ron clarifies he never agreed — she just appeared and started talking, and he accepted this as the current situation
jokes.explanation: Classic Ron/Leslie dynamic in a single line. Ron's deadpan correction — he didn't agree, she simply commenced — perfectly captures how their friendship works. Excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I used to give Leslie these incredibly specific tasks just to keep her busy. I'd say, 'Leslie, I need you to organize all the binders in this office by the number of sheets inside them, then cross-reference that with the color of the binder and create a spreadsheet.' She'd spend eight hours on it, and at the end of the day, I'd just throw it away.

jokes.text: Ron describes distracting an over-enthusiastic employee with a fake brochure: 'I once had you put together a brochure about different kinds of Indiana topsoil.'
jokes.setup: Ron is explaining his tactics for slowing Leslie down when she was too ambitious
jokes.punchline: The specific busy work was an Indiana topsoil brochure — absurdly dull and specific, revealed as deliberately meaningless
jokes.explanation: Works on two levels: Ron's elaborate government-employee time-wasting (deeply on-brand) and the specificity of topsoil as the dullest possible subject. The setup for the 'Mulch Ado About Nothing' callback makes it earn its keep.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I called it 'Much Ado About Mulching.' Get it? Because Shakespeare? And mulch?

jokes.text: Leslie: 'That soil brochure was not busy work. I mean, people still refer to Mulch Ado About Nothing.'
jokes.setup: Ron reveals the soil brochure was just fake busy work
jokes.punchline: 'Mulch Ado About Nothing' — a Shakespeare pun applied to a soil brochure, delivered with Leslie's complete sincerity about its cultural impact
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Mulch Ado About Nothing' is a perfect pun — clever without being forced — and the real joke is that Leslie not only named her soil brochure this, but genuinely believes it has ongoing cultural relevance. The combination of a genuinely good pun delivered with utter sincerity is textbook Parks and Rec excellence. High quotability, high rewatch value, deeply character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've been going to JJ's Diner every morning for 20 years. Waffles are a stable, predictable food. Consistent. Reliable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, those waffle mornings have been some of my favorite memories with you.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I know. That's why I keep doing them. But I go there for the waffles, not the company.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait... you're saying our special waffle tradition was just... about the waffles?

jokes.text: Ron: 'Those were distraction waffles?' Leslie: 'I thought they were friendship waffles.' Ron: 'Breakfast food can serve many purposes.'
jokes.setup: Ron reveals he used to take Leslie to JJ's Diner and distract her with waffles
jokes.punchline: Leslie is genuinely hurt that the waffles were tactical; Ron delivers the philosophical 'Breakfast food can serve many purposes' with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke. 'Friendship waffles' vs 'distraction waffles' is a perfect encapsulation of both characters — Leslie assigns warmth and meaning to everything (especially waffles), Ron operates on pure pragmatic strategy. Ron's philosophical rejoinder 'Breakfast food can serve many purposes' is delivered like an ancient proverb. It's funny, sweet, and deeply character-specific to both characters simultaneously. Extremely quotable and a rewatch highlight.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, I've been eating waffles since before you were born. They're just a delivery system for syrup and butter. I don't need them to change my life.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Breakfast food can serve many purposes.'
jokes.setup: Chris is devastated to learn his waffles were 'distraction waffles,' not 'friendship waffles.'
jokes.punchline: Ron delivers a philosophical pronouncement on breakfast food as if it's a profound truth from a Swanson family almanac.
jokes.explanation: Ron Swanson reducing Chris's emotional crisis to a stoic aphorism about breakfast food is perfect. 'Breakfast food can serve many purposes' sounds like something you'd find stitched on a Ron Swanson throw pillow — it's deadpan philosophy masking genuine emotional avoidance, which is his whole character.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: So this piece is about the commodification of the human form in late capitalism?

dialogue.speaker: Orin
dialogue.line: No, it's about the commodification of the human form in late capitalism AND the male gaze.

jokes.text: The Orin performance art scene: A host greets visitors with 'Howdy, neighbors. Welcome to human farm. Here's your animal feed. Please don't feed the animals.' A man is living as a farm animal in an exhibit.
jokes.setup: Tom and Ben arrive at what is clearly a bizarre performance art space
jokes.punchline: The mundane hospitality ('Howdy, neighbors') contrasted with the insane premise (a man living as a farm animal you can hand-feed)
jokes.explanation: The absurdist payoff to the earlier setup about Orin. The mundane greeting for an insane exhibit, and the polite instruction 'please don't feed the animals' for a human, makes the comedy work by treating the bizarre as completely normal.

jokes.text: Tom's reaction to Human Farm: 'Wow, this is really, really cool. I like the statement it's making that, you know, we're all in cages in a way.'
jokes.setup: Tom and Ben are at Orin's deeply unsettling performance art piece
jokes.punchline: Tom — not a deep thinker — immediately does the pretentious performance art interpretation correctly, which is the joke
jokes.explanation: Mild irony: Tom doing a genuinely insightful reading of the art. Functional but not especially sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: We need to address the molasses disaster victims with compassion and dignity.

dialogue.speaker: Jessica
dialogue.line: Absolutely. We should launch a comprehensive memorial initiative.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I'm thinking a candlelit vigil, a scholarship fund in their names...

dialogue.speaker: Jessica
dialogue.line: Or we could rebrand it as a 'Molasses Incident Awareness Month' with corporate sponsorships and a hashtag campaign.

jokes.text: Orin corrects Tom's interpretation: 'Yeah, it's actually about death and the city.' Tom: 'Yeah. I see that now.'
jokes.setup: Tom has given his interpretation of the art; Orin corrects it
jokes.punchline: Tom instantly pivots to 'Yeah, I see that now' — completely lacking the conviction of his original take, immediately deferring to the artist
jokes.explanation: Nice button on Tom's art-appreciation pretension. His immediate capitulation is believably Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, no, that's cool. Ben's great. Ben's really great. I'm happy for Ben.

jokes.text: Tom pitches to a Sweetums rep: 'I mean, you've already made history as the world's most beautiful CEO.'
jokes.setup: Tom is pitching a business partnership to a Sweetums executive
jokes.punchline: Tom's negotiation tactic is pure flattery — calling her 'the world's most beautiful CEO' as a serious business compliment
jokes.explanation: Functional Tom-hustler joke. He can't help being charming even in professional contexts. Not particularly special but in character.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: My real name isn't Jerry. It's Garry.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Garry? That's like a angry way to say Jerry.

jokes.text: The Sweetums rep explains the company is 'laying low' due to a molasses storage explosion that caused 'a slow-moving ecological disaster' — 'A lot of homes were very gradually flooded. People died.'
jokes.setup: The rep explains why Sweetums is currently keeping a low profile
jokes.punchline: The molasses disaster — a slow-moving flood, which is inherently funny as a physical concept — is delivered with bureaucratic casualness, including 'people died' said matter-of-factly
jokes.explanation: A slow-moving ecological disaster caused by molasses is genuinely clever dark comedy. The joke has layers: the inherent comedy of slow-moving molasses as a disaster, the corporate spin ('laying low'), and the casual 'People died' drop at the end. 'Well, all press is good press' / 'No, this was bad press' exchange also lands well. Dark subversive with excellent deadpan delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I've been thinking about becoming a cop, but I realized I don't know how to do a stakeout. Like, I don't even know what you're supposed to do on a stakeout.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You sit in a car and watch a location.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: For how long?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: As long as it takes.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's the problem. I can't just sit somewhere. I need to be doing something. I need to be moving around, talking to people, eating food.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Well, all press is good press.' Rep: 'No, this was bad press.'
jokes.setup: Tom tries to spin the molasses disaster positively
jokes.punchline: The rep flatly corrects the cliché — sometimes press really is just bad
jokes.explanation: A perfect economy joke. Tom's hustler optimism crashes against reality. The flat correction is exactly right.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Orin's art show was absolutely incredible. The way he captured the essence of despair and emptiness was just breathtaking.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, and I really appreciated how he used the color black. Very subtle choice.

jokes.text: The Sweetums rep offers Ben a job running their foundation while Ben is standing right there listening to Leslie get rejected: 'Just to clarify, it's a no to me on all fronts, and you're offering Ben a job?' / 'Yeah.' / 'Cool. Cool.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just been told Sweetums isn't interested in partnering with her; the rep then turns and offers Ben a job
jokes.punchline: Leslie's 'Cool. Cool.' — a perfectly calibrated expression of someone masking hurt and trying to be supportive while clearly dying inside
jokes.explanation: The repeated 'Cool. Cool.' is brilliantly economical — it does everything: shock, wounded pride, supportive-girlfriend mask, and comedic restraint all in two words. The situation is inherently funny (she organized this meeting and got rejected while her fiancé got a job offer) and the line perfectly captures Leslie's emotional intelligence trying and almost failing to manage the moment.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I trust Jeremy Jamm because he's the only person in this town who's more of a sociopath than I am.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Plus, he showed me his water flosser once and I was genuinely impressed.

jokes.text: Andy interrogates Jerry: 'Been looking at your file all day, Jerry — if that even is your real name.' Jerry: 'It's not. My real name is Gary.' Andy: 'Well, Gary — if that even is your real name—'
jokes.setup: Andy is conducting a serious detective-style interrogation of Jerry/Gary about the stolen computer
jokes.punchline: Andy's hard-boiled 'if that even is your real name' interrogation technique backfires — Jerry actually does have a different real name (Gary), and Andy simply repeats the tactic on the new name
jokes.explanation: Structurally excellent. The 'if that even is your real name' is a movie-detective cliché, and the joke is that it accidentally works — Jerry IS using a fake name — then Andy can't process the new information and just restarts the same skepticism on 'Gary.' The episode also deepens the running gag that Jerry's name is actually Gary. Airtight structure, high quotability.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm not wearing this stupid raccoon outfit.

dialogue.speaker: Orin
dialogue.line: But April, you're perfect as a raccoon. They're trash pandas.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Exactly. Why would you assign me that?

dialogue.speaker: Orin
dialogue.line: I'm a llama. Do you know how humiliating that is?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: At least llamas are cool. Raccoons are literally garbage.

dialogue.speaker: Orin
dialogue.line: We could trade.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No. You're staying a llama, and you're going to like it.

jokes.text: Andy explains his investigative logic: 'Okay, so we know it's not Jerry, unless he was lying to me. I can never tell when people are lying to me. Hopefully that doesn't come up in my police work.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just interrogated Jerry/Gary about the missing computer
jokes.punchline: Andy casually mentions his total inability to detect lies — a fatal flaw for a prospective cop — as a minor administrative concern
jokes.explanation: Andy's complete self-awareness about his incompetence — combined with his optimism that it won't matter — is perfectly delivered. 'Hopefully that doesn't come up in my police work' is the right level of Andy: he knows it's a problem, but he's pretty sure it'll be fine. Excellent structure and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm like the Beyoncé of government. Not in terms of talent or influence, but in terms of how many times I've been unfaithful to my wife.

jokes.text: Leslie attempts to distract April with an arts program idea: 'Maybe you should just drop everything and coordinate it.' April: 'I'm not stupid. What is that supposed to mean?' Leslie: 'It means that the only reason you brought me here is to distract me from the dog park.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has taken April to the Orin performance art show, ostensibly for fun, but really to distract her
jokes.punchline: April immediately sees through it — she points out the transparent manipulation
jokes.explanation: The callback to Ron's advice failing in practice. April is too smart (and too cynical) to be distracted by an arts program. Works as a character moment but not a standout joke.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ben, you were like the worst part of an inspirational movie. You know, the part where they explain the problem for forty-five minutes.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'You hate this show.' April: 'I love this show.' Leslie: 'What's your favorite part?' April: 'The heavy-handedness.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has accused April of hating Orin's performance art show to prove she only came to spy on Leslie
jokes.punchline: April's favorite thing about the show is 'the heavy-handedness' — a sophisticated, cynical art-criticism answer delivered completely deadpan, and it's the most April response possible
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. April is asked to prove she loves performance art and immediately produces 'the heavy-handedness' — a term that's both hilariously accurate about Orin's show and reveals April has been paying genuine critical attention while pretending not to care. Deeply character-specific, economical, and unexpectedly smart. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: The King's Speech is a terrible movie. It's basically two hours of a guy struggling to say words.

dialogue.speaker: Cameraman
dialogue.line: Yeah, but that's the best part.

jokes.text: April reveals she told Councilman Jamm about the dog park and he gave her 'a really cool dental mirror to check out my molars.'
jokes.setup: April has gone around Leslie to build political support for the dog park
jokes.punchline: Jamm — an orthodontist — gave April a dental mirror as a gift, and April found this genuinely cool
jokes.explanation: Jamm's character as an orthodontist who gives dental gifts is a nice detail. April finding it 'really cool' is both funny (she has weird taste) and slightly ominous (she's been corrupted by a corrupt politician).

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Chris, you're so incredibly handsome it's basically a crime.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Thank you?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, I'm serious. You're aggressively good-looking. It's unfair to the rest of us.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I... appreciate that, Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Your teeth are so white and perfect, it's honestly insulting. You're making everyone else look bad just by existing.

jokes.text: Orin at the Human Farm: 'Moo.' April: 'Moo.' Leslie: 'Quiet, weirdo.' April: 'Aren't you supposed to be a sheep?' Orin: 'No. You are.' April: 'Oh, shut up.'
jokes.setup: Orin is in character as a farm animal; Leslie, April, and Tom are having a fight nearby
jokes.punchline: Orin accuses April of being a sheep (i.e., following Leslie), which is actually thematically apt but also insane because a man in a cow costume is lecturing them on independence
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: the absurdity of Orin staying in character, the thematic accuracy of calling April a sheep, and the comedy of April engaging earnestly with a man performing as a cow.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, wait. So City Hall was actually robbed? Like for real?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: This is so cool! We've been practicing for this our whole lives and it finally happened!

jokes.text: Tom pitches Ben as a profile subject: 'This is a guy who's learned through an unbelievable series of bonehead business moves.' Ben winces.
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to sell Ben as a subject for a TV show.
jokes.punchline: His pitch essentially amounts to describing Ben as a failure — 'bonehead business moves' — delivered as if it's a selling point.
jokes.explanation: Tom's self-defeating salesmanship is a reliable bit, and the indignity for Ben is clear. Competent character comedy but not standout.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: There is no opposition. Jeremy Jamm is just a idiot who thinks he's important.

jokes.text: Tom pitches himself to a documentary filmmaker: 'Not to mention in the last month alone, three people have confused me for a shorter, Indian Ryan Gosling.'
jokes.setup: Tom is pitching himself as a documentary subject based on his business journey
jokes.punchline: He includes the Ryan Gosling comparisons as a credential — the specificity of 'shorter, Indian' makes it funnier and more Tomish
jokes.explanation: Pure Tom Haverford — self-aggrandizing with a specific physical self-awareness that's simultaneously modest and absurd. The qualifiers 'shorter, Indian' are what make it work; he's not claiming to be Ryan Gosling, just a specific regional variant.

jokes.text: Producer's reaction: 'That was my favorite part of the movie.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has compared Ben's TV presence to The King's Speech's stammer-heavy opening
jokes.punchline: The producer finds this compelling rather than off-putting — authenticity is the brand
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the previous joke. The producer's genuine enthusiasm for the King's-Speech-before-therapy comparison recontextualizes Leslie's insulting description as a selling point. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You lied to me about the entire thing.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: Psych!

jokes.text: Ben: 'What is happening?' — as yet another person offers him a job when he's supposedly committed to accounting.
jokes.setup: Ben keeps getting job offers throughout the episode despite having just accepted an accounting position
jokes.punchline: Ben's exasperated 'What is happening?' acknowledges how absurd the situation has become
jokes.explanation: Functional running gag acknowledgment. Works as a beat but doesn't add much new comedically.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: And that's why you never trust a Jamm.

jokes.text: Andy confronts Chris: 'Don't play stupid and handsome with me. You stole my computer so that I could practice for my police exam. You're as guilty as you are sexy.'
jokes.setup: Andy suspects Chris set up the computer theft as a police exam exercise
jokes.punchline: 'You're as guilty as you are sexy' — Andy complimenting Chris's attractiveness as part of an accusation, delivered as a logical equation
jokes.explanation: A genuinely excellent joke. 'Don't play stupid and handsome with me' is already a great inversion of the idiom, and 'you're as guilty as you are sexy' is a perfectly constructed non sequitur that makes complete logical sense in Andy's brain. It's deeply character-specific (Andy genuinely admires Chris), highly quotable, and shows strong comedic craftsmanship in the sentence construction.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: You just got jammed!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Oh my God, can you please stop saying that?

jokes.text: Chris reveals a second computer was actually stolen — it's a real crime. Andy: 'I can't tell if you're lying to me.' Chris: 'Really?' Andy: 'I think.' Andy: 'Like a real crime? That's even better.'
jokes.setup: Andy has been treating this as police practice; Chris reveals it's an actual robbery
jokes.punchline: Andy still can't determine if Chris is being truthful, and then pivots to excitement that a real crime is 'even better' than a practice one
jokes.explanation: The callback to Andy's inability to detect lies pays off immediately. 'I can't tell if you're lying to me / Really? / I think' is a great three-beat. And Andy's pivot to genuine excitement about the real crime is pure Andy optimism.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You eat mice. You eat mice and you always have.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I've seen you do it.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You're a mouse eater, Leslie.

jokes.text: Jamm at city council, asking who thinks parks are stupid: 'Who here thinks parks are stupid? Let the record show that everyone is raising their hands.'
jokes.setup: Jamm is maneuvering to sell Lot 48 to Paunch Burger instead of making it a park
jokes.punchline: He asks a loaded question in a city council setting and then documents the response as official record — using democratic process as a vehicle for his own corruption
jokes.explanation: Jamm's corrupt manipulation of city council procedure is played for comedy. The formality of 'let the record show' applied to a loaded question is the joke. Good character work for Jamm.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You better watch out, because I'm going to take you to the Octagon.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's where I'm going to destroy you.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: My ex-boyfriend used to say that all the time.

jokes.text: Jamm: 'You don't even have to be Asian to do math that simple.'
jokes.setup: Jamm has just laid out a financial argument for selling Lot 48 to Paunch Burger
jokes.punchline: The racist 'joke' reveals Jamm's character as a walking embodiment of small-town prejudice and corruption — the comedy is that he's this terrible
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Jamm is awful — the racism is there to establish him as a villain the audience can hate. It's character-based but relies on shock/offense rather than wit. The craft is in the deployment (making the antagonist maximally loathable) rather than the line itself.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know what? If someone steals my laptop, I'm gonna booby-trap my next one. You know, like Home Alone style.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's... that's illegal, Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What? It's my laptop!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You can't set traps that could seriously injure or kill someone.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Not even a little bit?

jokes.text: Jamm to April: 'Uh, psych.' Then: 'You just got jammed.'
jokes.setup: April is confronting Jamm about his betrayal — he promised to support the dog park
jokes.punchline: 'Psych' followed by 'You just got jammed' — Jamm has a self-aggrandizing catchphrase for his betrayals
jokes.explanation: Jamm's self-appointed catchphrase 'You just got jammed' is a running gag that works because it's so self-satisfied and petty. 'Psych' is an anachronistic choice (90s slang from Jamm) that fits his character perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm gonna be the greatest police officer this town has ever seen. I'll solve crimes with my bare hands, rappel down buildings, maybe even fight a robot.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Andy, you haven't even passed the police academy yet.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Details, Jerry. Details.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I hate when he says that.'
jokes.setup: Jamm has just delivered 'You just got jammed'
jokes.punchline: Leslie's flat, defeated reaction implies this has happened before — 'jammed' is a recurring indignity in her life
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — six words do the character work of implying a whole history. Leslie has been jammed before. She is tired of being jammed. This is her life.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I don't know if police work is for me. Maybe I'm not cut out for this.

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. What happened to the Andy Dwyer who came in here full of energy and optimism?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: He's still here, he's just... discouraged.

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: Well, we're going to treat this like any other case. I'm going to need you to describe what was taken.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: Your confidence. Someone stole your confidence. And we're going to find them.

jokes.text: Leslie to April: 'You deceived me for two straight days, and you eat mice.' April: 'I don't eat mice.' Leslie: 'Yes, you do. You're a mouse eater. Mouse eater. Mouse eater.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and April are having a serious argument about deception and professional respect
jokes.punchline: Leslie escalates from a legitimate grievance to the completely unfounded accusation that April eats mice, then repeats 'mouse eater' in a chant
jokes.explanation: A great absurdist detour during a serious argument. The accusation of mouse-eating comes from nowhere (Leslie comparing April to a snake leads to snake-prey logic) and the triple repetition of 'mouse eater' as a chant is Leslie at peak irrational. Deeply specific and original — this joke could only happen in this episode.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Accounting is not boring. If accounting were a TV show, it would be on HBO, not some basic cable network. It would have complex characters, intricate plotlines, and it would make you think.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, accounting would be on C-SPAN at 3 AM, and it would still get better ratings than C-SPAN's usual programming.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's fair.

jokes.text: Ben: 'Enough! You are friends and coworkers. In this office, we treat each other with respect.' / Jerry walks in. / 'Hey, April, how is that dog park coming?' / Leslie and April: 'Get out, Jerry!' / 'This is private!' / Jerry: 'Sorry, guys.'
jokes.setup: Ben has just delivered a sincere speech about mutual respect
jokes.punchline: Jerry's completely oblivious entrance immediately gets him kicked out by both parties — the one thing Leslie and April agree on is Jerry doesn't belong here
jokes.explanation: Ben's speech about respect is immediately undermined by both women uniting to reject Jerry — a perfect structural joke. The moment of unity around Jerry-exclusion is exactly the character comedy that makes Parks great. Jerry's cheerful obliviousness makes it work even more.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: A&E doesn't cover boring topics.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: They have a show called 'Storage Wars.'

jokes.text: Ron agrees to guard the meeting room door: 'No one leaves the Octagon.' / Leslie: 'I dated an ultimate fighter. It was like a thing he said.'
jokes.setup: Ben asks Ron to guard the door so Leslie and April can work things out
jokes.punchline: Ron gravely declares 'No one leaves the Octagon' with full seriousness, then Leslie provides the context that she dated an MMA fighter and this was his thing
jokes.explanation: Ron's deadpan intensity applied to a government hallway is funny, and the explanation that he got this from Leslie's fighter ex is a nice background detail. The 'It was like a thing he said' casualness is good deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: We need to play dirty with Jamm.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Okay, I'll go roll around in the mud.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: No, that's not what I meant.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Too late, I'm already covered in mud.

jokes.text: Andy's crime-solving plan: 'You're gonna set up a perimeter, maybe bug a few phones? Ooh, I know. We could put out a dummy computer for them to steal, fill it with explosives first, boom, take 'em all out.'
jokes.setup: Andy wants to run a full investigation into the computer theft
jokes.punchline: Andy's escalating plan goes from standard police procedure to suggesting they blow up the thieves with a bomb — delivered as a completely reasonable escalation
jokes.explanation: Andy's escalation from 'set up a perimeter' (normal) to 'fill it with explosives first, boom, take 'em all out' (murder) as a logical continuum is great Andy comedy. The 'boom' sound effect he does himself is the detail that makes it.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. If I'm sad, I need to take off my shirt because the sadness needs to escape through my torso.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: And if I'm happy, I gotta keep it on so the happiness doesn't fly away.

jokes.text: Officer: 'Look, man, this is what most police work is. Just writing stuff down. It's not superhero time.' Andy: 'Maybe we should find the person who stole his positive attitude.'
jokes.setup: The officer is delivering a realistic speech about the mundanity of police work to temper Andy's expectations
jokes.punchline: Andy's response to a man losing his enthusiasm for his job is to suggest a new crime: the theft of a positive attitude
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed joke. Andy takes the metaphor of someone 'losing' their enthusiasm and literalizes it — treating it as an actual theft requiring investigation. It's an excellent Andy-logic moment that's also oddly sweet and perfectly worded. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Dude, I'm gonna get a gun! I'm gonna be packing heat!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Actually, security guards in Indiana aren't authorized to carry firearms without additional licensing and training that this position doesn't provide.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So... no gun?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: No gun.

jokes.text: Ben downplays his new accounting job: 'Well, my accounting job isn't boring. If it was remotely interesting, there would be a show on A&E about it.'
jokes.setup: Tom says maybe he should take a cue from Ben and stick to his 'boring day job'
jokes.punchline: Ben defends accounting by... confirming it is indeed boring, using A&E programming as the standard for interestingness
jokes.explanation: Ben's self-deprecating defense of accounting is funny because he's defending it by conceding it's boring, using A&E's reality TV slate as the baseline. The logic is perfect Ben-nerd energy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Oh my God! Oh my God! They're doing it right there on my lawn! In broad daylight! This is... this is a disaster! My neighbors are going to think I'm running some kind of... of... animal brothel!

jokes.text: Tom: 'They have a show about storage unit auctions.' Ben: 'Fair point.'
jokes.setup: Ben has said accounting isn't interesting enough for A&E
jokes.punchline: Tom points out A&E literally has a show about storage unit auctions — an extremely low bar — and Ben concedes the point immediately
jokes.explanation: Quick and economical. Tom's observation is accurate (Storage Wars is real), and Ben's instant capitulation is funny. Works as a button.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, so we all agree that Jeremy Jamm is the worst, right?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Obviously.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: He's terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I've been thinking about his stupid catchphrase, 'Treat Yo' Self.' What if we created our own versions?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Like what?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: 'Treat Yo' Staff.' Because we should treat our staff well.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: 'Treat Yo' Health.' Get a checkup.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: 'Treat Yo' Pets.' Because animals matter.

jokes.text: Ben: 'Also can you tell me what time that show about storage units is on?' Tom: '9:30.'
jokes.setup: Ben has just been debating whether accounting is interesting enough for A&E
jokes.punchline: Ben, in the middle of advising Tom on his business, asks about the storage unit show's airtime — revealing he actually wants to watch it
jokes.explanation: Great button — Ben condemning himself with his own curiosity. 'And Tom knows immediately without hesitation' is also funny. Ben the nerd wanting to watch storage auction TV is perfectly embarrassing.

dialogue.speaker: Jamm
dialogue.line: I won! Treat yo' self!

jokes.text: April's apology: 'I'm sorry that I outsmarted you at every turn.' Ben: 'April.' April: 'And I know I have a lot to learn from you, and I'm sorry that I disrespected your stupid dream.'
jokes.setup: Ben is trying to get April to sincerely apologize to Leslie
jokes.punchline: April's apology is technically an apology but contains 'outsmarted you at every turn' and 'your stupid dream' — she cannot bring herself to be fully sincere
jokes.explanation: A perfect April moment. She's genuinely trying to apologize but her character literally won't allow full sincerity — so the apology is loaded with backhanded qualifiers. 'I'm sorry that I outsmarted you at every turn' is one of the best April lines in the episode. Deeply character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You just had a baby. Shouldn't you be home enjoying your family?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Enjoy? April, I don't understand. There are zoning permits that need reviewing.

jokes.text: Ann: 'I hate Paunch Burger, but if there is one in my backyard, I will eat there, like, every night, and that is no good.'
jokes.setup: The group is strategizing about how to stop Jamm from selling Lot 48 to Paunch Burger
jokes.punchline: Ann's motivation for opposing Paunch Burger is entirely self-protection — she knows her own weakness
jokes.explanation: Ann's relatable honesty about her inability to resist fast food near her house is a good self-aware moment. Not spectacular but grounded and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm quitting accounting. I'm going to start my own business venture.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You've got to spend money to make money. It's just business 101.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Yes. We'll have triple-sex with him.' Ann: 'No. I have an idea... it is a dick move.' Leslie: 'I love it.'
jokes.setup: Ann says they need to start playing dirty with Jamm
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately jumps to 'triple-sex' as the obvious play — Leslie's brain apparently goes there first — then the actual plan is described as merely a 'dick move'
jokes.explanation: Leslie's immediate leap to 'triple-sex' is a good character subversion — the eternally professional Leslie's mind going there first. Leslie saying 'I love it' before she even hears the plan is also a good character beat.

jokes.text: Andy's latest suspect: 'My new suspect — the dude who runs carpet emporium. The way I figure it, criminals love to wrap things up in rugs. Plus, he yelled at me when I tried to unroll 'em all.'
jokes.setup: Andy is providing an investigation update; he has a new suspect
jokes.punchline: His reasoning is (1) criminals use rugs to wrap bodies (a movie trope) and (2) the rug store owner was annoyed when Andy started unrolling all his merchandise
jokes.explanation: Andy's detective logic is perfectly calibrated — he's working from movie-crime logic and the rug store owner's totally reasonable frustration is being interpreted as guilt. The specificity of 'unroll 'em all' implies Andy really did this, which is its own funny story.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm leaving accounting to pursue something more fulfilling.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Do you know what I'm giving up? Dental. Full dental coverage. And vision. What if I go blind? I need to see things!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: And the 401k match — they match up to 6%! Six percent! That's free money! Who leaves free money?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh God, I just realized I lose my parking spot. My spot. The one by the entrance.

jokes.text: Andy taking his shirt off when sad: 'When I get bummed out, I take my shirt off because the bad feelings make me feel sweaty.'
jokes.setup: Andy is visibly demoralized about potentially giving up his police dreams
jokes.punchline: His coping mechanism — removing his shirt because feelings make him sweaty — is completely nonsensical but delivered with total internal logic
jokes.explanation: A very Andy-specific quirk — the cause-and-effect logic ('feelings make me sweaty, so no shirt') is perfectly absurd. The performance of this line (presumably with Andy visibly starting to remove his shirt) amplifies it significantly.

jokes.text: Chris offers Andy the weekend security guard job: 'But keep in mind, if you take this job, you must keep your clothes on at all times, even if you get sad.' Andy: 'No deal.' / 'Okay, I'll do it.'
jokes.setup: Chris is offering Andy a practical way to explore a law enforcement career
jokes.punchline: The job offer has a specific no-shirt clause; Andy initially refuses on principle, then immediately capitulates
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff. The shirt clause is necessary and specific, Andy's 'No deal' is a serious position, and then he immediately folds. The rapid reversal — 'No deal.' / 'Okay, I'll do it.' — is perfectly timed. Builds beautifully on the shirtless bit.

jokes.text: Andy: 'And I get a gun, and I can point it in people's faces.' Chris: 'Incorrect.'
jokes.setup: Andy accepts the security guard job and immediately starts negotiating perks.
jokes.punchline: He assumes gun-pointing is part of the job. Chris's one-word correction — 'Incorrect' — is the perfect response.
jokes.explanation: 'Incorrect' is an ideal single-word punchline — it corrects Andy's deranged assumption with maximum economy. The juxtaposition of Andy's excited specificity ('point it in people's faces') against Chris's flat 'Incorrect' is the whole joke, executed cleanly.

jokes.text: Andy: 'And I get a gun, and I can point it in people's faces.' Chris: 'Incorrect.'
jokes.setup: Andy is confirming the terms of his new security guard job
jokes.punchline: Andy's main expectation is gun access and face-pointing; Chris corrects this with a single word
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy. Andy's sincere belief that pointing a gun at people's faces is the job, and Chris's clinical 'Incorrect' — not 'no' or 'absolutely not' but the formal, disappointed 'Incorrect' — is perfect. One of the episode's most quotable exchanges.

jokes.text: Leslie and April's plan: releasing dogs and children on Jamm's front lawn. A dog is 'dry-humping my garden gnome.'
jokes.setup: The plan to pressure Jamm is bringing dogs and kids to play on his property
jokes.punchline: One dog is dry-humping Jamm's garden gnome, which Jamm is specifically outraged about
jokes.explanation: The specific detail of the garden gnome and the dog's behavior is a strong visual gag. Jamm's specific outrage about the gnome over the general chaos is a good character note — he cares about weird things.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Yeah, sic the police on a bunch of kids and puppies. That's a great photo op.'
jokes.setup: Jamm threatens to call the police on the children and dogs on his lawn
jokes.punchline: Leslie points out the political optics of arresting kids and puppies — this is her best weapon
jokes.explanation: Leslie's political instincts are always her superpower. Using 'kids and puppies' as optics leverage is competent Leslie comedy. Not especially original but well-placed.

jokes.text: After the deal: 'You just got knoped. And ludgated.' / 'And perkinsed.' / 'Ha-ha. Nice try. It didn't work.' / Jamm: 'You just got jammed.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and April have successfully maneuvered Jamm into a 90-day deal — they try to coin their own catchphrases
jokes.punchline: Their self-named catchphrases don't land ('Nice try, it didn't work'), but Jamm still gets 'You just got jammed' in because he won the last word even in defeat
jokes.explanation: A structurally excellent bit: Leslie and April try to mirror Jamm's catchphrase victory, it falls flat (meta-humor about catchphrases not working on demand), and then Jamm squeezes in 'You just got jammed' anyway because he's that guy. The Ann addition of 'perkinsed' and its immediate failure is the cherry. Callback with a twist.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Wait, wait, wait, do you never just take a second to enjoy things?' April: 'I just said, let's get to work.' Leslie: 'How else do people enjoy things?'
jokes.setup: Leslie immediately says 'let's get to work' after their victory
jokes.punchline: April, usually the cynic, is advising Leslie to enjoy the moment — but then Leslie's idea of enjoyment is still work-adjacent, as evidenced by 'How else do people enjoy things?'
jokes.explanation: A sweet final character note for Leslie and April's relationship. April playing the 'slow down' role she learned from Leslie while Leslie is already head-down working is a nice inversion. 'How else do people enjoy things?' is a deeply Leslie question — she genuinely doesn't know another way.

jokes.text: Ben quits his accounting job again. His boss: 'Is this a classic Ben joke?' Ben: 'No. I'm really sorry.' Boss: 'This is disappointing. Again.'
jokes.setup: Ben has seemingly started the accounting job and is now in the office — then he quits again
jokes.punchline: The boss has experienced this before ('Again'), implies there's a pattern, and even has a name for it: 'a classic Ben joke'
jokes.explanation: The 'classic Ben joke' framing implies these people have built a whole taxonomy around Ben's behavior. 'This is disappointing. Again.' with the pause before 'Again' is beautifully timed. These accountants know Ben too well.

jokes.text: After Ben quits again, his boss calls for Ted: 'Ted, get in here! Ben's quitting again, but you gotta hear what he said.'
jokes.setup: Ben's boss has just heard Ben's goodbye speech
jokes.punchline: Instead of being upset, Barney is excited to share what Ben said with Ted — implying Ben's quitting has become entertainment for the accounting office
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Ben's departures have become an event the office looks forward to is a great comedic button. Barney calling for Ted to hear it implies this is a known office phenomenon. Economical and a great character beat for the accounting firm as a setting.

jokes.text: Ben's speech about why he's quitting: 'I mean, why be an accountant, you know? Other than the stability and the health plan and the above-average pay.'
jokes.setup: Ben is giving himself a pep talk about following his passions
jokes.punchline: He undercuts his own inspirational moment by immediately listing all the genuinely good reasons to stay — stability, health plan, above-average pay — acknowledging the full cost of his choice
jokes.explanation: The self-aware undercut of his own inspiration is very Ben. He makes the brave choice but is also a pragmatist who fully acknowledges what he's giving up — and listing those things out loud is both funny and a little sad. Great structure: inspire yourself, immediately second-guess. Character-specific and economical.

jokes.text: Ben's boss: 'Maybe someday we'll figure out the magic formula that gets you to work here.' Ben: 'Well, formulas are my formula for moolah.'
jokes.setup: The boss is expressing hope that Ben will return; Ben tries to sign off with a pun
jokes.punchline: 'Formulas are my formula for moolah' — a deliberately bad pun that doesn't quite make sense, Ben trying to deliver a callback to his 'municipal bond' nerd energy
jokes.explanation: A deliberately weak pun — 'formulas are my formula for moolah' barely makes semantic sense — but that's somewhat the point: Ben is in a weak emotional state and his nerd puns aren't landing even by his low bar. Less funny than the municipal bond joke but consistent.

jokes.text: Ben's final talking head: 'Oh, God, this better work out.'
jokes.setup: Ben has just delivered a speech about following his passions
jokes.punchline: The camera catches his private fear immediately after his public bravery — 'Oh, God, this better work out' is the real Ben
jokes.explanation: The perfect episode-closing beat for Ben's arc. It's economical (six words), character-specific (Ben's pragmatist anxiety), and structurally sound (inspirational speech immediately followed by private panic). 'Oh, God' as an opener for a confessional is perfectly Ben. Highly quotable episode button.

tmdb_overview: Leslie gets upset when April tries to get Lot 48 made into a dog park. Meanwhile, Tom enlists Ben's help as he tries to launch his new business venture, and Andy hones his crime scene investigation skills.
insight: Leslie-April conflict fuels 67 jokes in 24 minutes, anchoring Season 5's tonal shift.
